blocks.text: There is a notable passage on the peacock in 1 Reg. X, 22. and 2 Par. IX, 21.: Once every three [col. 136] years the fleet (of Solomon) went to Tarshish, and brought gold and silver, elephants' teeth, apes and peacocks. The Hebrew name of the peacocks, תכיים thoucijim, or תוכיים thuccijim, the Greek translators left ἀνεϱμήνευτον [anermēneuton] [untranslated], because they did not understand it. But the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Latin translators explain it as peacocks, and so do all the Hebrews of any repute: R. Selomo, R. Levi, Kimchi, Pomarius, Aquinas. For those who, in Kimchi's Lexicon, render it גאטו מימון gato maimon, that is, long-tailed monkey, are obscure and unknown. So too are those who render it parrot, as Junius notes in the margin ^{(1)}. Therefore I cannot at all understand why the late Diodati preferred to follow them. It is hardly safe to depart from the received version unless there are weighty reasons, and I see none here. On the origin of the word, Mercerus says in his Thesaurus: The word seems foreign, for its etymology is unknown. Perhaps it is from striking, by onomatopoeia. The French, to be sure, express onomatopoeically the sound of someone knocking at a door with the words toc, toc; hence toquer means to strike, as does toccare in Italian. But since such things are largely arbitrary: among the Hebrews תוך תוך thoc thoc is said of the sound of a boiling pot. Thus in Berachoth ch. 6, fol. 39a: דיתיב אבי תפי ועביד תוך תוך, That which is placed in the place of setting (of pots on the fire), and makes thoc thoc. But however you understand it, this has nothing to do with the peacock. Nor can any reason be devised why it should be named from striking. I therefore hold a different view: namely, that peacocks are called תוכיים thuccijim by an inversion of the word, for כותיים cuthijim, as if you were to say Cuthaeans, or Persians. For Cuth (var. Chuth) is in Persia. Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, near the end: Οἱ δὲ μετοικισθέντες εἰς Σαμάρειαν Χουθαῖοι (ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐχρῶντο μέχρι δεῦρο τῇ προσηγορίᾳ, διὰ τὸ ἐκ τῆς Χουθᾶς καλουμένης χώρας μεταχθῆναι, αὕτη δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ ποταμὸς τοῦ τ᾽ ἔχων ὄνομα) [Hoi de metoikisthentes eis Samareian Chouthaioi (tautē gar echrōnto mechri deuro tē prosēgoria, dia to ek tēs Chouthas kaloumenēs chōras metachthēnai, hautē d᾽ estin en tē Persidi, kai potamos tou t᾽ echōn onoma)]. The Cuthaeans deported into Samaria (for so they were then called, because they had been transferred from the region of Chutha, which is in Persia, where there is also a river of the same [II, 710] name). Nor is it anything new for birds to be named after places. Thus the pheasant is named from the Phasis; African and Numidian birds from Numidia and Africa; Seleucides from Seleucia; Garamantides from the Garamantes. And, not to seek examples further afield, the very peacock we are discussing is often called the Median or Persian bird by the ancients. Aristophanes in the Birds:
Ὁ μὲν ὄρτυγα δοὺς, ὁ δὲ πορφυρίων᾽, ὁ δὲ χῆν᾽, ὁ δὲ Περσικὸν ὄρνιν᾽ [Ho men ortyga dous, ho de porphyriōn᾽, ho de chēn᾽, ho de Persikon ornin᾽]

One giving a quail, another a porphyrion, another a goose, another a Persian bird. And there the Scholiast: Τὰ πολυτελῆ πάντα, οἷς μόνος βασιλεὺς ἐχρῆτο, ἐκαλεῖτο Περσικά· καὶ νῦν οὐκ ἰδίως τις ὄρνις Περσικός. τινὲς δὲ τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα, οἱ δὲ τὸν ταῶ [Ta polytelē panta, hois monos basileus echrēto, ekaleito Persika; kai nyn ouk idiōs tis ornis Persikos. tines de ton alektryona, hoi de ton taō]. All costly things, which the king alone used, were called Persian. Some, however, understand the cock, and others the peacock. And in the Acharnians, of the Persian envoys:
Ἥκοντες ἀπὸ Περσίδος ταὼν ἔχοντες ἐληλύθασιν, [Hēkontes apo Persidos taōn echontes elēlythasin,]
